items.prompt: What is the main difference between a bee nest and a beehive?

options.label: A nest is made of wax, a hive of wood
options.feedback: Both nests and hives contain honeycomb made of wax; the difference is not the material but who made the structure.

options.label: A nest is used for young, a hive for honey
options.feedback: Both nests and hives house the young and store honey; they serve the same functions.

options.label: A nest is natural, a hive is man-made
options.feedback: Correct. A nest is built by the bees in a natural or artificial cavity or hanging exposed, while a hive is a structure made by humans to house a colony.

options.label: A nest is above ground, a hive is underground
options.feedback: Nests can be in caves, rock cavities, hollow trees, or hanging exposed; hives are artificial but not necessarily underground.

items.ok_line: A nest is where bees house themselves; a hive is a human-made home for them.
items.ko_line: The difference is the builder, not the function or location.
items.exp_text: A beehive is an enclosed structure in which honey bees raise young and produce honey. But the word 'nest' refers to colonies that house themselves in natural or artificial cavities or in hanging exposed structures, while 'hive' is used for a man-made structure created to house a honey bee colony. So the key is that a nest is made or chosen by the bees, a hive is made by people.

items.prompt: Which two species of honey bees are the main ones kept in artificial beehives?

options.label: Western and eastern honey bees
options.feedback: Correct. The western honey bee (Apis mellifera) and the eastern honey bee (Apis cerana) are the main species kept in artificial hives.

options.label: Bumblebees and carpenter bees
options.feedback: These are not kept in hives in the same way; they are different groups from the honey bees of the genus Apis.

options.label: Africanized and European honey bees
options.feedback: These are not listed in the reference as the main species; they are not mentioned at all.

options.label: Worker and drone honey bees
options.feedback: Workers and drones are castes within a single species, not separate species kept in hives.

items.ok_line: Western and eastern honey bees are the ones commonly put in hives.
items.ko_line: These choices are either different bee types or castes, not the two named species.
items.exp_text: Species of Apis live in colonies, but the western (Apis mellifera) and eastern honey bees (Apis cerana) are the main species kept in artificial beehives. These two are the ones bred and housed by beekeepers for honey and pollination.

items.prompt: What material are the cells of a honeycomb made of?

options.label: Tree resin
options.feedback: Tree resin is used to make propolis, which coats cavity walls, but the comb itself is not made of resin.

options.label: Pollen
options.feedback: Pollen is stored inside the cells but is not the building material of the comb.

options.label: Mud and straw
options.feedback: Mud and straw are used in traditional hives as the outer enclosure, not for the comb cells.

options.label: Beeswax
options.feedback: Correct. The honeycomb is a densely packed group of hexagonal prismatic cells made of beeswax.

items.ok_line: Bees build their comb out of wax they produce themselves.
items.ko_line: The cells are made of beeswax; the other materials either line the nest or fill the cells.
items.exp_text: The hive's internal structure is a honeycomb—a densely packed group of hexagonal prismatic cells made of beeswax. These cells store food and house brood.

items.prompt: Where in the comb do honey bees store honey, and where do they raise worker brood?

options.label: Honey at the bottom, worker brood at the top
options.feedback: It is the reverse: honey goes in the upper part of the comb, and worker brood is below the pollen-storage cells.

options.label: Honey in the upper part, worker brood below the pollen
options.feedback: Correct. The standard architecture places honey in the upper part, then rows of pollen-storage cells, worker-brood cells, and drone-brood cells in that order.

options.label: Honey on the sides, worker brood in the middle
options.feedback: The arrangement is vertical, not side to middle; the order is honey at top, pollen next, then brood.

options.label: Honey and worker brood mixed together randomly
options.feedback: Honey bees keep a consistent order, not a random mix, to organize the nest.

items.ok_line: Honey sits on top, pollen below it, and worker brood beneath that.
items.ko_line: The comb is arranged in layers from top to bottom, not by mixing or by sides.
items.exp_text: In a honeycomb, honey is stored in the upper part; beneath it are rows of pollen-storage cells, worker-brood cells, and drone-brood cells, in that order. This keeps food and young in a set arrangement.

items.prompt: What do honey bees use propolis for in their nest?

options.label: To make the comb cells sticky for storing honey
options.feedback: Propolis is not used in comb construction; it coats the cavity walls, not the cells.

options.label: To seal the queen cell so the larva cannot escape
options.feedback: Propolis is not mentioned as sealing queen cells; it is a general coating for cavity walls.

options.label: To coat the cavity walls with a thin hardened layer
options.feedback: Correct. Bees smooth the bark around the entrance and coat the cavity walls with a thin layer of hardened plant resin called propolis.

options.label: To attract pollen to the cells
options.feedback: Propolis does not attract pollen; pollen is brought in by foragers, not summoned by resin.

items.ok_line: Propolis coats the walls to harden and protect the cavity.
items.ko_line: Propolis is a wall lining, not a comb material or pollen lure.
items.exp_text: Honey bees often smooth the bark around the nest entrance and coat the cavity walls with a thin layer of hardened plant resin called propolis. This is separate from the comb, which they build out of wax.

items.prompt: What shape are the cells that bees build in their honeycomb?

options.label: Hexagonal prisms
options.feedback: Correct. The cells are hexagonal prismatic shapes made of beeswax.

options.label: Round spheres
options.feedback: Cells are not round; they have flat walls meeting in hexagons.

options.label: Square boxes
options.feedback: The cells are not square; they have six sides, making them hexagonal.

options.label: Triangular pyramids
options.feedback: The cells have six sides, not three, and they are prism-shaped, not pointed.

items.ok_line: Each cell is a hexagonal prism, a six-sided tube.
items.ko_line: Hexagonal means six sides; round, square, or triangular all have different numbers of sides.
items.exp_text: The honeycomb is described as a densely packed group of hexagonal prismatic cells made of beeswax. Hexagonal means six-sided, and prismatic means they are long and tube-like.

items.prompt: Where do honey bees typically build their queen cells?

options.label: At the very top of the comb
options.feedback: The top holds honey, not the queen cells; those are lower down.

options.label: At the lower edge of the comb
options.feedback: Correct. The peanut-shaped queen cells are normally built at the lower edge of the comb.

options.label: In the middle of the pollen-storage rows
options.feedback: Pollen rows are for pollen storage; queen cells are separate and at the lower edge.

options.label: Outside the hive, on the entrance
options.feedback: Queen cells are inside the comb, not on the hive's outside walls or entrance.

items.ok_line: Queen cells sit at the bottom edge of the comb.
items.ko_line: The lower edge is the location, not the top, middle, or outside.
items.exp_text: The peanut-shaped queen cells are normally built at the lower edge of the comb. This is distinct from honey, pollen, and worker or drone brood, which occupy the rest of the comb.

items.prompt: What natural sites do honey bees use for nesting?

options.label: Underground burrows
options.feedback: Honey bees do not dig burrows; they use caves, rock cavities, and hollow trees.

options.label: Open fields with tall grass
options.feedback: They need enclosed cavities or exposed hanging structures, not open fields.

options.label: Abandoned bird nests
options.feedback: They do not use bird nests; they choose caves, rock cavities, or hollow trees.

options.label: Caves, rock cavities, and hollow trees
options.feedback: Correct. Honey bees use these natural cavities as nesting sites, and in warmer climates may build exposed hanging nests.

items.ok_line: Bees nest in caves, rock cavities, and hollow trees.
items.ko_line: Honey bees prefer enclosed natural cavities, not burrows, fields, or other nests.
items.exp_text: Honey bees use caves, rock cavities, and hollow trees as natural nesting sites. In warmer climates they may build exposed hanging nests, with multiple parallel honeycombs and a single entrance.

items.prompt: In a traditional hive with no internal structures, what happens to the honeycomb?

options.label: It is built in neat, movable frames
options.feedback: Movable frames are modern equipment, not traditional; traditional hives have no provided structures.

options.label: It is attached to the top and can be lifted out whole
options.feedback: In traditional hives the comb is cross-attached and cannot be moved without destroying it.

options.label: It is cross-attached and cannot be moved without damage
options.feedback: Correct. Because no internal structures are provided, the bees create comb that is often cross-attached, so moving it destroys it.

options.label: It is built outside the hive on a branch
options.feedback: The comb is built inside the hive, not outside, even if the hive has no frames.

items.ok_line: Traditional hives have comb that is attached in place and breaks if moved.
items.ko_line: Without internal supports, the comb grows randomly and is fragile to move.
items.exp_text: Traditional beehives, also called fixed-frame hives, provide no internal structures. The bees create their honeycomb within, and it is often cross-attached so it cannot be moved without destroying it. This is why harvesting often destroys the hive.
